title: Ezekiel 16:1–14
context: The LORD tells the prophet, whom he addresses as “Son of man,” to make Jerusalem know her abominations, and gives a long allegory of the city as a woman. Jerusalem's origins are traced to the land of Canaan, and she is pictured as an abandoned newborn whom no one pitied. The LORD passes by, commands her to live, raises her, enters into a covenant with her, and adorns her with royal splendor. Her beauty is “through my majesty which I had put on you.” The point of this opening section is the LORD's unearned kindness, which sets up the charge of unfaithfulness that follows. These notes speak of the allegory soberly and keep its referent, Jerusalem, in view.

verses.text: Again the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: “Again the LORD’s word came to me.” Arminian readers note that this begins one of the longest messages in Ezekiel, an extended allegory addressed to Jerusalem through the prophet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same opening and that the allegory follows the parable of the vine. Both chapters speak to Jerusalem's confidence and the LORD's coming judgment.

verses.text: “Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations;
verses.arminianNotes: “Son of man, cause Jerusalem to know her abominations.” Arminian readers see the purpose of the message: to bring the city to see its sin clearly, which is a necessary step toward repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD names the referent at once: the allegory is about Jerusalem. Exposure of sin is the LORD's work through his word, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: and say, ‘The Lord GOD says to Jerusalem: “Your origin and your birth is of the land of the Canaanite. An Amorite was your father, and your mother was a Hittite.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your origin and your birth is of the land of the Canaanite.” Arminian readers see the LORD reminding Jerusalem that she had no noble beginning to boast of: “An Amorite was your father, and your mother was a Hittite.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the language is not a genealogy of individuals but a moral portrait. Jerusalem's roots were among the peoples of Canaan, so her later standing came wholly from the LORD.

verses.text: As for your birth, in the day you were born your navel was not cut. You weren’t washed in water to cleanse you. You weren’t salted at all, nor wrapped in blankets at all.
verses.arminianNotes: “As for your birth, in the day you were born.” Arminian readers see a newborn left without the basic care a child would receive. The picture stresses Jerusalem's helplessness before the LORD acted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note how the details emphasize total neglect. Nothing was done for the child, which highlights that what follows is the LORD's initiative alone.

verses.text: No eye pitied you, to do any of these things to you, to have compassion on you; but you were cast out in the open field, because you were abhorred in the day that you were born.
verses.arminianNotes: “No eye pitied you.” Arminian readers see the child “cast out in the open field,” unwanted by anyone, as a picture of Jerusalem's lowly and desperate beginnings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the absence of human compassion sets the stage for divine compassion. Both traditions see here the undeserved nature of the LORD's love.

verses.text: “ ‘ “When I passed by you, and saw you wallowing in your blood, I said to you, ‘Though you are in your blood, live!’ Yes, I said to you, ‘Though you are in your blood, live!’
verses.arminianNotes: “When I passed by you.” Arminian readers see the LORD's life-giving word, “Though you are in your blood, live!” as gracious initiative toward the helpless, calling for a response of gratitude and faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same command as a sovereign word that gives life to one who could not help herself. Many draw an analogy to regeneration, while both traditions agree the verse first describes the LORD's care for Jerusalem.

verses.text: I caused you to multiply as that which grows in the field, and you increased and grew great, and you attained to excellent beauty. Your breasts were formed, and your hair grew; yet you were naked and bare.
verses.arminianNotes: “I caused you to multiply as that which grows in the field.” Arminian readers see the LORD's care causing the child to grow and flourish, though she was still without covering or status.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that growth comes from the LORD's hand. The allegory moves from rescue to maturity, preparing for the covenant that follows. The notes leave the imagery in its allegorical setting.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Now when I passed by you, and looked at you, behold, your time was the time of love; and I spread my garment over you and covered your nakedness. Yes, I pledged myself to you and entered into a covenant with you,” says the Lord GOD, “and you became mine.
verses.arminianNotes: “I spread my garment over you.” Arminian readers see the LORD taking Jerusalem as his own: “I pledged myself to you and entered into a covenant with you.” Covenant love calls for faithful love in return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Ruth 3:9, “spread the corner of your garment over your servant,” as a picture of protection and commitment. The LORD's covenant makes Jerusalem his: “you became mine.”

verses.text: “ ‘ “Then I washed you with water. Yes, I thoroughly washed away your blood from you, and I anointed you with oil.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then I washed you with water.” Arminian readers see the LORD cleansing and caring for his covenant people, removing the marks of their former abandonment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the washing and anointing are entirely the LORD's acts. Many see a picture of grace that cleanses before it adorns, while keeping the allegory focused on Jerusalem.

verses.text: I clothed you also with embroidered work and put leather sandals on you. I dressed you with fine linen and covered you with silk.
verses.arminianNotes: “I clothed you also with embroidered work.” Arminian readers see lavish provision: fine linen, silk, and leather sandals, showing the LORD's generosity toward his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the clothing is costly and royal. The LORD does not merely rescue Jerusalem but honors her, which makes her later misuse of these gifts all the more serious.

verses.text: I decked you with ornaments, put bracelets on your hands, and put a chain on your neck.
verses.arminianNotes: “I decked you with ornaments.” Arminian readers see bracelets and a chain as gifts that display the LORD's delight in his people and their exalted place among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that every ornament is given, not earned. Both traditions see here the generosity of God, which becomes the backdrop for the charge of ingratitude in verse 15.

verses.text: I put a ring on your nose, earrings in your ears, and a beautiful crown on your head.
verses.arminianNotes: “a beautiful crown on your head.” Arminian readers see the LORD raising Jerusalem to royal dignity, with ring and earrings completing her adornment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the crown fits the next verse's statement that she “prospered to royal estate.” Many connect this with the kingdom of David and Solomon, though the allegory does not name them.

verses.text: Thus you were decked with gold and silver. Your clothing was of fine linen, silk, and embroidered work. You ate fine flour, honey, and oil. You were exceedingly beautiful, and you prospered to royal estate.
verses.arminianNotes: “Thus you were decked with gold and silver.” Arminian readers see abundance: fine food of “fine flour, honey, and oil,” and a people who “prospered to royal estate” through the LORD's blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that food and clothing alike come from the LORD. Verses 17–19 will show these same gifts misused, so the list here prepares for the indictment.

verses.text: Your renown went out among the nations for your beauty; for it was perfect, through my majesty which I had put on you,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your renown went out among the nations for your beauty.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem's fame as a gift meant to display the LORD's goodness to the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the phrase “through my majesty which I had put on you.” Her beauty was borrowed glory. Both traditions treat this as shared ground: whatever Jerusalem had, she had received.
